title: Moab's Pride and God's Lament
summary: The longest of Jeremiah's oracles against the nations announces the ruin of Moab, Israel's neighbor east of the Dead Sea. Town after town is named as the destroyer sweeps across the plateau, and Moab's god Chemosh goes into exile with his priests, because Moab trusted its wealth and magnified itself against the LORD. Yet the poem is full of grief, with God himself wailing for Moab, and it ends with a promise that in the latter days he will restore Moab's fortunes.
story: After Egypt (chapter 46) and the Philistines (chapter 47), the oracles turn east to Moab. Moab's story was bound up with Israel's from the beginning: Genesis traces the Moabites to Lot, Abraham's nephew (Genesis 19:37); Moab's king hired Balaam to curse Israel on the plains before the conquest (Numbers 22 to 24); and Ruth, the great-grandmother of David, was a Moabite. The two peoples fought often, and Moab mocked Israel in its humiliation (verse 27). This chapter declares that Moab, long secure and proud, will share the fate it scorned. Its unusual length and its deep notes of lament make it one of the most striking of all the oracles. Chapter 49 continues with Ammon, Edom, and others.
historical:
Moab occupied the high plateau east of the Dead Sea, roughly between the Arnon gorge and the Zered valley, with good land for grain, vineyards, and sheep. Much of what we know about Moab outside the Bible comes from the Mesha Stele (also called the Moabite Stone), a black basalt inscription found in 1868 at Dhiban, the biblical Dibon (verses 18 and 22). Set up around 840 BC by Mesha king of Moab (2 Kings 3:4-5), it credits the god Chemosh with freeing Moab from Israelite control, and it names several towns that appear in this chapter, among them Nebo, Kiriathaim, Dibon, Aroer, Jahaz, and Horonaim. It also contains one of the earliest known references outside the Bible to Israel's God, whose sacred vessels Mesha claims to have taken from Nebo.

The chapter gives no date for Moab's fall. Moab was a vassal of Babylon in Jeremiah's time and was represented at the meeting of western kings in Jerusalem that Jeremiah warned against (27:3). The Jewish historian Josephus, writing in the first century AD, says Nebuchadnezzar made war on Moab and Ammon in his twenty-third year, about 582 BC. Whatever the exact events, Moab as an independent kingdom disappears from the record during the following centuries, its territory absorbed by Arab peoples and later by the Nabataeans.
cultural:
Chemosh was the national god of Moab, as the LORD was Israel's God; the Moabites are called "The people of Chemosh" (verse 46), and Numbers 21:29 uses the same phrase. Solomon built a high place for Chemosh near Jerusalem (1 Kings 11:7), which Josiah later defiled (2 Kings 23:13). When a nation was conquered, its god's statue was often carried off with its priests (verse 7), a public sign that the god had been defeated.

The image in verse 11 comes from winemaking. New wine was left on its dregs, the sediment of yeast and grape skins, to develop flavor, then poured from jar to jar to separate it from the sediment. Wine left too long on its dregs became thick and harsh. Moab had never been poured out into exile, and so it had settled into a complacent, unchanged character (compare Zephaniah 1:12). The mourning rites in verse 37 (shaved heads, clipped beards, gashed hands, sackcloth) and on the rooftops and public squares (verse 38) were the region's customary signs of grief. The vine of Sibmah and the winepresses (verses 32 and 33) remind the reader that Moab was known for its vineyards.
literary: The chapter is a long poem made of shorter units, and much of it is shared with other parts of the Old Testament. Verses 29 to 38 closely parallel Isaiah's oracle on Moab (Isaiah 15 and 16), verses 43 and 44 echo Isaiah 24:17-18, and verses 45 and 46 adapt an old victory song from Numbers 21:28-29 and Balaam's oracle in Numbers 24:17. Scholars debate how these passages are related, but the effect is to gather Israel's long tradition about Moab into one piece. The poem is marked by lists of place names (verses 1 to 5, 21 to 24, 31 to 34), which create a sense of destruction sweeping over the land town by town. Its most surprising feature is the voice of God in lament: "Therefore I will wail for Moab" (verse 31) and "My heart laments like a flute for Moab" (verse 36). The final verse turns suddenly to hope, and a closing note marks the end of the section.

outline.t: Destruction sweeps the towns of Moab
Moab settled on its dregs will be poured out
Judgment on the high plain and on Moab's mockery
No escape: terror, pit, and snare
In the latter days Moab restored

doctrines.note: Moab trusted "in your works and treasures" (verse 7) and in Chemosh, and both will fail. Just as Israel was ashamed of trusting the shrine at Bethel (verse 13), Moab will be ashamed of its god.
The root of Moab's judgment is pride: "he has magnified himself against the LORD" (verse 26). Verse 29 piles up six words for arrogance, showing that pride is the central sin being judged.
God judges Moab, yet he grieves over it: "My heart laments like a flute for Moab" (verse 36). Divine judgment in this chapter is not cold; it comes with sorrow.
The chapter ends with a promise that God will restore Moab in the latter days (verse 47). Even a nation under judgment is not beyond his purposes of mercy.

words.note: Kemosh, Chemosh, the national god of Moab. He is named three times in the chapter (verses 7, 13, 46). The Mesha Stele shows Moab believed Chemosh fought for them and gave them victory. The chapter declares that he will go into exile, unable to save his people or himself.

Shemer, the dregs or sediment of wine. Moab has settled like wine on its dregs (verse 11), never disturbed and so unchanged. The image suggests that ease and security had produced complacency, and that the pouring out of exile would disturb it.
Gaon, pride or majesty. The same word can be used positively of God's majesty, but when applied to people it often means arrogance. Moab's pride (verse 29) is the chapter's central charge.

Shevut, captivity or fortunes. The phrase in verse 47 is often translated to restore the fortunes. It is the same phrase Jeremiah uses for Israel's restoration (30:3). That God would use it for Moab is a remarkable sign of his mercy beyond Israel.

christ: The chapter ends with God's promise to restore Moab in the latter days. Moab was the nation of Ruth, the woman who left her people to follow Israel's God and became the great-grandmother of David, and Matthew names her in the genealogy of Jesus (Matthew 1:5). The New Testament presents the gospel as God's blessing reaching all the nations, as he promised Abraham. The link here is thematic rather than predictive: the chapter shows that God's purpose for the nations includes restoration after judgment, a hope the church sees fulfilled as people from every nation come to Christ. The divine lament over Moab also anticipates the grief of Jesus, who wept over the city that rejected him even as he announced its judgment.

hard.q: How can verse 10 curse anyone who holds back the sword from bloodshed, while God himself weeps for Moab?
hard.a: Verse 10 is one of the harshest lines in Jeremiah, and it sits uneasily beside God's lament in verses 31 to 36. Interpreters read the verse as a statement about the certainty of God's judgment: the agent God has appointed, in context most likely the Babylonian army, must carry out its task fully, and half-hearted obedience to God's command is itself condemned (compare Saul in 1 Samuel 15). It is not a general command to believers to shed blood. Many readers also point out that the chapter holds together two things the Bible often keeps in tension: God's judgment is real and certain, and God takes no pleasure in it (Ezekiel 18:32). Some interpreters find the tension unresolved and say so, while others see it as a true picture of divine justice and grief together. The chapter doesn't ask readers to celebrate Moab's destruction; it asks them to see both God's justice and his sorrow.

questions: Moab settled like wine on its dregs, unchanged because it had never been disturbed. How can comfort and security make a person or a community complacent?
Moab mocked Israel in its humiliation and later faced the same fate. What does this chapter teach about how we treat others when they fall?
God weeps for Moab even while judging it. How does that change the way you think about God's justice?
